overview: Most beds that die here didn't fail because of the plants. They failed because of what's under them. So every install starts with prep: a clean bed line that won't wander into the lawn, every weed pulled by the root, the top of the soil loosened, compost worked into heavy clay, and a grade that moves water off instead of letting it sit around the plants.

Then we plant for where you live. Perennials and shrubs give the bed its backbone, annuals rotate the color, and native and pollinator plants go in where they fit. Everything is laid out so the bed reads from the street and from the porch. We finish with mulch at the depth that works here and a crisp edge, so it looks the same in August as it did the day we left.

timing: Shrubs and perennials do best planted in fall, September through November, while the soil is warm and the air is cooling. Heat lovers like vinca should wait until the soil is truly warm, usually mid-May and later, because a cool, wet spring rots them. Seasonal color rotates with the weather, so the bed has something blooming most of the year.

east_texas.title: Plants that make it through a Longview July
text: A Longview summer means weeks in the high 90s, a heat index past 105, humidity that breeds fungus, and clay that bakes hard between rains. Petunias and impatiens look great in April and are crispy sticks by the Fourth of July. That's a plant-choice problem, not a green-thumb problem.

In full sun we reach for lantana, vinca, salvia, plumbago and knockout roses, with dwarf yaupon and dianthus in the mix. Azaleas and hydrangeas work where they're sited right. Most of these hate wet feet, so we build beds that drain and tell you to water deep and less often. Daily watering in clay is how a lot of good plants get killed.

faq.q: How much does a new flower bed cost in Longview, TX?
faq.a: Flower beds fall under our landscaping and planting work, where most projects run $900 to $3,600. A small refresh of an existing bed starts at a few hundred dollars. The size of the bed, how many plants and what size, the edging material and how much prep the soil needs set the price. We walk it for free and send a written, itemized quote.

faq.q: What flowers survive the summer in East Texas?
faq.a: In full sun, lantana, annual vinca, salvia, plumbago and knockout roses hold their color through July and August. All five want sun and good drainage and hate being overwatered. Lantana and plumbago are often root-hardy here and come back in spring. Vinca should wait for warm soil, usually mid-May on, or it can rot in a cool, wet spring.

faq.q: Why did my new flower bed die in its first summer?
faq.a: Usually it's the plant choice or the prep, not you. Spring annuals like petunias and impatiens aren't built for our heat. Beds set on compacted clay with weeds left underneath struggle from day one, and daily watering in clay drowns roots. Most beds we redo for clients failed on the prep step. The plants were fine. The soil they sat in wasn't.

faq.q: Do you put landscape fabric under flower beds?
faq.a: No. Mulch breaks down into soil every year, and on top of fabric that new layer becomes a perfect seed bed. Weeds root right through the sheet, and in year three you're tearing out shredded fabric. We edge the bed clean, prep it well and mulch at 1 to 1.5 inches. Fabric belongs under rock, not under mulch.

faq.q: Can I see a design before you plant?
faq.a: Yes. The $199 Flower Bed Preview gets you a rendering of the bed, a plant list with sizes, the bed shape and edging spec, and one round of revisions. It's built for bare front beds, foundation plantings and single-bed refreshes. The fee is credited toward a qualifying install booked within 90 days.
